presentingComplaint: Two days of high fever with rigors, painful urination and perineal pain
history: A 58-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of abrupt-onset high-grade fever with shaking chills, dysuria, urinary frequency and urgency, poor stream with a sense of incomplete emptying, and a dull aching perineal/pelvic pain radiating to the low back. He reports pain on defecation. Background of benign prostatic hyperplasia on tamsulosin; type 2 diabetes on metformin. No recent instrumentation, but a prior episode of cystitis 6 months ago. No urethral discharge and no new sexual partners.
examination: Ill-looking, flushed, febrile. Abdomen soft; suprapubic fullness with mild tenderness and a palpable bladder suggesting partial retention. Digital rectal examination reveals an exquisitely tender, warm, boggy and swollen prostate. No fluctuant mass to suggest abscess. No costovertebral angle tenderness. Testes and epididymes non-tender; no urethral discharge; no genital ulcer or rash.

labs.urinalysis: pyuria (WBC 60/hpf), positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites, bacteriuria
labs.PSA: not indicated acutely (falsely elevated in acute inflammation)

imaging: Not routinely indicated in classic acute bacterial prostatitis; bedside bladder scan shows post-void residual ~180 mL. Transrectal ultrasound/CT reserved for suspected prostatic abscess (persistent fever >36 h on appropriate therapy).
microbiology: Midstream urine culture sent (pending); blood cultures x2 drawn before antibiotics. Prostatic massage is contraindicated in acute prostatitis. Most likely Escherichia coli; other Enterobacterales (Klebsiella, Proteus) and Enterococcus possible.
differentialDiagnoses: Complicated lower UTI / cystitis with retention
citations: Harrison 22e — Urinary Tract Infections, Pyelonephritis, and Prostatitis
IDSA/AUA Prostatitis (acute bacterial prostatitis) management, contemporary guidance 2010-2022
stewardship: Empiric fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin) which achieves good prostatic penetration; in acutely inflamed gland a beta-lactam (e.g. ceftriaxone) is also acceptable given inflammation increases penetration, especially where local fluoroquinolone resistance in E. coli is high (relevant in India). Cover Enterobacterales; add empiric coverage per local resistance. Total duration 2-4 weeks to prevent chronic prostatitis. De-escalate on culture and sensitivity.
contraindications: Fluoroquinolone caution: tendinopathy, QT prolongation, aortic aneurysm risk; avoid if allergy
Adjust ciprofloxacin/beta-lactam dose for renal function
Avoid nitrofurantoin/fosfomycin - poor prostatic tissue penetration
edgeCases: Failure to defervesce within 36-48h suggests prostatic abscess requiring imaging and drainage, especially in diabetics/immunocompromised
Acute urinary retention may require suprapubic (preferred) rather than urethral catheterisation to avoid pressure on the inflamed gland
In young sexually active men consider N. gonorrhoeae/C. trachomatis and treat accordingly
expectedMaiK: Classic acute bacterial prostatitis: febrile lower-UTI syndrome in a man with an exquisitely tender boggy prostate on DRE. Avoid prostatic massage, cover Enterobacterales with a prostate-penetrating agent (fluoroquinolone or, in the inflamed gland, a beta-lactam) for a prolonged 2-4 week course, and watch for abscess or retention.
